title: Pyne warns AI could be 'means of human race's destruction'

By Paul Johnson

7.30

Topic:AI

Former Labor leader Bill Shorten has called for a slowdown of AI development. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Former Labor leader Bill Shorten and former Coalition defence minister Christopher Pyne have joined the chorus for a slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence (AI).

Both issued blunt warnings on 7.30 about the damage AI could do without guardrails, as Mr Shorten compared AI to nuclear weapons and called for an AI version of the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NNPT).

That treaty was introduced in 1970 to stop the spread of nuclear weapons, promote peaceful use of nuclear energy and pursue negotiations towards disarmament.

"I think the more that we hear from the CEOs and the chief officers of these frontier laboratories of AI, I cannot help escape the conclusion that we may have built nukes with opinions," Mr Shorten told 7.30.

"This is a marvellous technology, but until we can regulate it, we need to slow down.

"What we're seeing at the cutting edge of AI laboratories is actually a technology which doesn't appear to need humans to make decisions. Once you eliminate human oversight, there's no guarantee that what we're designing will actually make decisions in the best interest of humanity."

Mr Shorten said he wasn't suggesting that building data centres or infrastructure was a problem, but that generative AI needed more human oversight.

Mr Pyne, who holds several positions as a strategic advisor and consultant, including in the defence industry, echoed the sentiment.

"AI has tremendous opportunity for the human race. It has the capacity to make our lives much, much better, not just from a health perspective, but many others," Mr Pyne said.

Former Liberal MP Christopher Pyne runs lobbying firm Pyne & Partners. (Four Corners: Ryan Sheridan)

"But there is an inherent danger.

"Obviously, human beings are the smartest beings on the planet; we have dominion over the globe because we might not be the strongest, we might not be the fastest, but we're the smartest.

"And we've created something that's actually smarter than us and, with regenerative self-improvement, is going to get much smarter and much quicker than we ever can.

"So we could have actually created the means of the human race's destruction.

Pressed if that was something he expected, Mr Pyne pulled back.

"I'm an optimist. I think it will all be OK in the end, but we wouldn't want to underestimate what we've done," he said.

With that warning, the pair were asked what could be done to bring the rapid development of AI under control.

It is the same question those in the industry have been facing.

CEO and Co-Founder of Anthropic Dario Amodei has called for a slowdown on AI advancement. (Reuters: Denis Balibouse)

First AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who left OpenAI to join Anthropic, decided to leave the industry, accusing both US companies of "gambling with our lives" in the race to develop models capable of self-improvement.

That sparked a deluge of calls to slow it down from Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the "godfather of AI"; Anthropic boss Dario Amodei; OpenAI head Sam Altman; and Elon Musk, who owns xAI.

"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models," Mr Amodei wrote in a post on his personal website.

Given the nuclear comparisons made earlier, Mr Shorten was asked if an AI version of the NNPT was needed.

"Dario [Amodei] has proposed a plan, which does involve independent verification," Mr Shorten said.

"It does involve, as technologies are being developed, that you have external observers, like we have the International Atomic Energy Agency.

"So I do think it does need global action and I don't think we can afford, in Australia, to say the problem is someone else's.

"As a middle power, we can help lead this debate, but it's pretty interesting that you have the technology leaders, the private sector, saying, 'Hey, we need help here. We need regulation.'

"So I do think there is some analogy between the proliferation of nuclear weapons and the proliferation of AI and maybe some of the solutions that were used for nuclear weapons need to be put into place here."

Mr Pyne agreed, and while he said AI was a race between the US and China, he suggested that guardrails were necessary to prevent potential rogue actors from being involved.

"China and the United States are locked in a competition over AI for different reasons, and it could be very dangerous," he told 7.30.

"But by the same token, we as humans need to live on this planet and we need them to come to an agreement that the rest of the world can then fold into."

With immigration dominating the political agenda after One Nation released its policy earlier in the week, the two former senior politicians were asked what should be done.

Tony Burke was due to outline Labor's migration policy last month, but postponed the speech. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Mr Shorten, Vice-Chancellor of the University of Canberra, acknowledged the government had work to do but cautioned against acting too harshly, especially on mooted changes to policy around international students.

"We don't need to be in a bargaining auction in a race to the bottom about the lowest possible number," he told 7.30.

"We need migrants for this country to do well. Migrants tend to pay; as a group, they're more likely to pay tax."

He said cutting international student numbers could become an economic nightmare.

"If some people are overstaying their visas, by all means clamp down, but economic self-harm when it comes to cutting international students is a real problem.

"It's international students whose fees cross-subsidise us being able to support Aussie kids. It's international students' fees that allow us to fund research, which the nation wouldn't otherwise get.

Bill Shorten is vice-chancellor at the University of Canberra. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

"And in regional Australia … if you take out international students, there will be job losses.

"So governments have got to have a migration debate, but it's not going to save a government or an opposition."

Asked for his take on the issue, Mr Pyne said: "Migration has built this country.

"Everything Bill said about international students is right.

"Saying that we're going to start curtailing international students is definitely an act of self-harm.

"What politicians need to do is actually start standing up for migration, a population that is sustainable and explaining the benefits that this brings.

"Australia is so powerful internationally because of its multiculturalism and all the people in Australia who do business with the countries that they came from or their grandparents came from because of the knowledge they have, the skills they gain, the language commonalities.

"These things are not something that we should be embarrassed about."
